content:
This is the first installment of our latest autumnal series, exploring the rich folklore woven along the Pacific Crest Trail. As we travel up and down the trail, we’re sharing the local legends, traditions, and passed-down myths in its deep cultural fabric that connect generations of the community. For the oddities you can’t quite explain and the encounters that felt almost otherworldly, this series is for you. Written by Alisha Grauso. 

Of all the cryptid legends of North America, none is better known or more widespread than Bigfoot, a.k.a. Sasquatch.

Photo by James Parsons

Though Bigfoot-like creatures aren’t unique to North America–stories of similar wild “hairy men” exist in virtually every part of the globe–the elusive creature is arguably best associated with the Pacific Northwest and surrounding territories. After all, it’s the famous (or infamous, depending on how you feel about it) Patterson-Gimlin film shot in Northern California in 1967 that established the iconic silhouette of Bigfoot, with its long stride and loose, swinging arms.

Hardly a modern invention of the internet, as are entities such as the rake and Slender Man, stories of Bigfoot can be found in the legends of virtually every single Indigenous tribe in North America, whether the Tlingit of the Pacific Northwest or the Cherokee people who were the original Appalachians. Those stories depict both peaceful and adversarial relations with the wild people, old accounts of native tribes trading with their primal neighbors, whom they largely considered to be another race, and even some legends that describe Indigenous tribes and Sasquatch once sharing a common tongue.

However, encounters with the elusive creature aren’t just relegated to the realm of ancient Indigenous folklore. Their history has continued unbroken for centuries. Accounts from hikers and campers encountering Sasquatch on and around the PCT exist into the current day.

Take, for example, this witness account submitted to the BFRO last year about an encounter that happened in September 2024 in Washington, about 24 miles NE of Mount Rainier. The witness and her fiancé were hiking to the emergency cabin in Government Meadows off the Horse Camp Trail in Greenwater. As they approached the trail, they saw three dark, hairy figures–two adults, one carrying a smaller one on its back–cross the trail below and hurry into the woods.

Accounts like this litter the Pacific Crest Trail’s history.

Photo by: Colin Arisman

They range from observed sightings and physical encounters, including the well-documented phenomenon of rock throwing, to more mundane stories of hearing tree knocks and howls. And while your chances of encountering Bigfoot in desert climates and more populous settings are low, most encounters seem to cluster around mountains.

Like Mount Rainier, Mount Shasta is one of those documented hotspots for Sasquatch encounters, an arguably unshocking revelation considering the mountain’s long history of high strangeness. The Indigenous tribes of the region all treat the mountain as sacred and eerie, and their practices reflect their respect for the strange mountain and the entities that inhabit it. The Shasta people, for example, will not go above the treeline of Mount Shasta, claiming it is the realm of gods and the spirits of the dead; only their strongest shamans venture above the treeline.

Backcountry wilderness also seems to attract the elusive ape-like figures.

“Around Mount Shasta, monsters roam the forests. They creep here and there, they say, and every time you turn your back, you don’t know what might be watching.”
Photo by: Chris Pickering

With the Pacific Crest Trail running through six different national parks on its meandering path from the deserts of Southern California to the rugged rainforests of the PNW, it’s no surprise that those parks are rife with stories of encounters. Hike the PCT long enough, and you’re bound to run into a fellow nature lover who has spent time in Yosemite or the Olympia Peninsula and has some strange stories to tell.

Whether one believes those tales or not–or, like Fox Mulder, wants to believe–the indisputable truth is that there are enough stories of Sasquatch sightings that an entire cottage industry of Bigfoot tours and investigations has popped up in and around the PCT. One Washington county, Skamania, even established a law in 1969 (later revised in 1984) that makes it illegal to kill a Sasquatch.

Bigfoot is as intertwined with the land as the mountains and trees, older than our national parks, older than the Pacific Crest Trail, older, even, than our stories about them. Just knowing there’s a possibility that they exist injects a little bit of wonder into a trail that already generates so much.

It gives us even more of a reason to be responsible stewards of the PCT–after all, it’s what good neighbors do.

“A fun Bigfoot meter gauge in Oregon”
Photo by: Laurie Meade
